goal: Pick one task from your current job or the job you want. You'll run it through three assistants today.

steps.label: Write your goal
steps.why: Every lab starts with your own task so the work matters to you.
do: Think of one task you do (or will do) regularly: a weekly report, answering customer emails, planning a schedule.
Type it in one or two sentences in the box below. Be specific: 'Summarize my team's weekly sales numbers into a short update' beats 'reporting'.
steps.see: A one or two sentence goal in the box. That's it.

checkpoint.prompt: Your task, in one or two sentences
checkpoint.placeholder: Example: Draft replies to the five most common customer questions at my store.

steps.label: Create your three accounts
steps.why: You'll compare the three big assistants side by side all course long.
do: Open chatgpt.com and click Sign up. Use your Google account to skip a password.
Open claude.ai and do the same.
Open gemini.google.com. It signs in with the same Google account automatically.
Leave all three tabs open.
steps.see: Three browser tabs, each with an empty chat box and a blinking cursor.
steps.tip: If a site asks for a phone number, that's normal for the free tier. If you'd rather not, ask your instructor for the class backup account.

checkpoint.prompt: All three tabs are open and I can type in each one.

steps.label: Write three questions
steps.why: Writing questions before you ask stops the assistant from steering you.
do: Open a new Google Doc and title it 'Week 1 Day 1 comparison'.
Write three questions about your task that you'd ask an experienced coworker. One factual (what is...), one how-to (how would I...), one judgment (should I...).
Number them 1, 2, 3.
steps.see: A doc with your goal at the top and three numbered questions.

steps.label: Ask all three assistants
steps.why: Same question, three answers. The differences are the lesson.
do: Copy question 1. Paste it into ChatGPT, press Enter. Paste the same text into Claude and Gemini.
Under question 1 in your doc, paste each answer with a label: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini.
Repeat for questions 2 and 3.
steps.see: Nine answers in your doc, three under each question. Some will be long; that's fine.
steps.tip: If an assistant asks you a clarifying question instead of answering, type 'Just give me your best answer' and continue.

checkpoint.prompt: Quick check: the three assistants gave different answers to the same question. Why?
options: They predict likely text from different training and settings, so there's no single 'correct' output
checkpoint.why: Each assistant predicts the next words from its own training and settings. Different models, different predictions. None of them looked anything up unless you saw a 'searching' indicator.

steps.label: Mark what's wrong or vague
steps.why: Spotting the weak spots is the skill. Trusting output blindly is the trap.
do: Read each answer. Highlight in yellow anything that's wrong, made up, or so vague it doesn't help.
If an answer looks perfect, reply to the assistant: 'What's your source for that?' and highlight anything it can't back up.
Aim for at least one highlight per assistant.
steps.see: Yellow highlights across your doc. At least three total.

checkpoint.prompt: Describe the worst mistake you found and which assistant made it
checkpoint.placeholder: Example: Gemini said my state's sales tax is 4% but it's 8%.

steps.label: Sort eight real applications
steps.why: This is Domain 1 of the exam: knowing which kind of problem is which.
do: Decide whether each is Regression (predicts a number), Classification (picks a category), or Clustering (finds groups without labels):
Fraud detection · Sales forecasting · Movie recommendations · Spam filter · House price prediction · Grouping customers by behavior · Photo tagging · Demand planning
Write your eight answers, one per line, with a short reason.
steps.see: Eight lines. Typical answers: fraud = classification, forecasting = regression, recommendations = clustering or classification, spam = classification, house price = regression, customer groups = clustering, photo tagging = classification, demand = regression.

checkpoint.prompt: Grouping customers by shopping behavior, with no labels given, is:
checkpoint.why: No labels and the goal is to find natural groups: that's clustering. Classification needs labeled categories to learn from.

steps.label: Upload your doc
do: Take a screenshot of your comparison doc showing at least one highlighted answer, or set the doc to 'Anyone with the link can view' and copy the link.
Upload it below.
steps.see: A thumbnail of your screenshot, or your link, in the submissions list.

checkpoint.prompt: Screenshot or link to your comparison doc

stretch: Ask each assistant to describe its own limits, then fact-check one claim it made about itself using an official source
Rewrite your weakest question so all three assistants give a useful answer
doneWhen: Three assistants, nine answers, at least three highlights
All eight applications sorted with one reason each

submission.prompt: Upload a screenshot of your comparison doc, or paste a link to it.

lens.term: AI, ML, deep learning, generative AI
lens.plain: The nesting dolls. AI is the umbrella, machine learning learns rules from examples, deep learning stacks many layers, generative AI creates new content.
lens.exam: Domain 1: distinguishing AI, machine learning, deep learning, and generative AI.

lens.plain: Narrow AI does one kind of task very well. AGI would do any mental task a person can. Only narrow AI exists.
lens.exam: Not in any Domain. The exam only tests today's narrow AI; AGI and ASI never appear. Know the difference so the word "AI" in a question never makes you think of robots or sci-fi.

lens.plain: A model plus tools plus a loop that decides its next step.
lens.exam: Domain 1, Objectives 1.1.1 and 1.1.2: define agentic AI and tell it apart from AI, ML, GenAI, and deep learning. Also 1.2.4 (real-world applications) and Domain 3, 3.1.6 (the role of AI agents in business).

lens.plain: Sorting into categories vs predicting a number.
lens.exam: Domain 1: real-world use cases by problem type.

lens.plain: You need an exact repeatable answer, there's not enough good data, or the cost outweighs the value.
lens.exam: Domain 1: when AI/ML is and isn't appropriate.

quiz.q: Which statement about the AI family tree is correct?
a: Machine learning is a type of generative AI
Deep learning sits inside machine learning, which sits inside AI
Generative AI replaced machine learning in 2022
AI and machine learning are the same thing
quiz.why: AI is the umbrella. Machine learning is inside it, deep learning inside that, and generative AI is built on deep learning.

quiz.q: A pharmacy needs the exact same tax calculation every time. Why is AI the wrong tool?
a: AI is too expensive for pharmacies
AI gives plausible answers, not guaranteed exact ones
AI can't do math at all
quiz.why: When you need an exact, repeatable answer every time, a rule or formula beats a model that predicts.

quiz.q: Predicting next month's sales figure is an example of:
quiz.why: Regression predicts a number. Classification sorts into categories. Clustering finds groups.

quiz.q: What makes an AI system an agent rather than a chatbot?
a: It can take actions with tools and decide its next step
quiz.why: An agent is a model plus tools plus a loop that decides what to do next.

quiz.q: Your bank's app rounds every purchase up to the nearest dollar and saves the change. Is that AI?
a: No, it's a rule a person wrote, with the same result every time
No, because banks don't use AI
quiz.why: The test is whether the machine learned its rules from examples or a person wrote them. Rounding is a written rule. Same input, same output, forever. Banks do use AI elsewhere, like fraud detection, which learns from examples.

tools.use: General assistant for the three-way comparison

cards.q: What is artificial intelligence, in one sentence?
cards.a: Software that does a task we'd normally say takes human thinking: recognizing, predicting, deciding, or generating. It's the umbrella term; everything else tonight sits under it.

cards.q: What is machine learning, and how is it different from ordinary programming?
cards.a: Ordinary programs follow rules a person wrote. Machine learning finds the rules itself by looking at many examples. You give it data and answers, it works out the pattern.

cards.q: What makes deep learning different from other machine learning?
cards.a: Deep learning uses a neural network with many layers, so it can learn from raw messy input like pixels or audio without a person picking out the features first. It's a type of ML, not a separate thing.
AI that produces new content (text, images, code, audio) instead of only sorting or predicting. Most of it is built on deep learning. ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini are generative AI.
AI that takes actions toward a goal over several steps: it plans, uses tools like search or email, checks results, and keeps going. A chatbot answers; an agent does.

cards.q: How do AI, machine learning, deep learning, and generative AI fit together?
cards.a: Nested circles. AI is the biggest. Machine learning is inside AI. Deep learning is inside machine learning. Generative AI is mostly built on deep learning. Agentic AI uses generative models and adds actions.

cards.q: What's the difference between a model and an algorithm?
cards.a: The algorithm is the recipe for learning. The model is what comes out after the algorithm has learned from data: the thing you actually use to make predictions.

cards.q: What's the difference between training and inference?
cards.a: Training is the learning phase: the model studies examples and adjusts. Inference is the using phase: the trained model gets new input and gives an answer. Training happens once (or occasionally); inference happens every time you use it.

cards.q: When is a problem a classification problem?
cards.a: When the answer is a category or label: spam or not spam, which of five product types, approve or deny. The output is a choice from a fixed set.

cards.q: When is a problem a regression problem?
cards.a: When the answer is a number on a scale: next month's sales, a house price, how many minutes a delivery will take. The output is a quantity, not a category.

cards.q: When is a problem a clustering problem?
cards.a: When you have no labels and want the computer to find natural groups on its own, like sorting customers into segments nobody defined in advance. The groups come from the data.

cards.q: When is AI the wrong tool for a job?
cards.a: When you need the exact same correct answer every time (a tax calculation, a rounding rule), when a simple rule already works, or when the cost of building and running it outweighs the benefit. AI predicts; it doesn't guarantee.

cards.q: What three kinds of value does AWS say AI/ML brings to a business?
cards.a: Helping humans decide (surfacing patterns a person would miss), scaling a solution to volumes people can't handle, and automating repetitive work. If a scenario mentions one of these, AI/ML is probably appropriate.

cards.q: Name five everyday applications that count as AI on the exam?
cards.a: Computer vision (reading images), NLP (understanding text), speech recognition, recommendation systems, fraud detection, and forecasting. Knowledge bases and agentic AI were added in 2026.

practice.q: A company's marketing team says they're 'using AI' because a tool writes first drafts of their emails. The data team says they're 'using AI' because a model predicts which customers will cancel. Which statement is MOST accurate?
a: Only the marketing team is using AI; prediction isn't AI.
Only the data team is using AI; writing text isn't AI.
Both are using AI. The marketing tool is generative AI and the prediction model is machine learning.
Neither is using AI unless the tools use deep learning.
practice.why: AI is the umbrella. Generating text is generative AI; predicting churn is classic machine learning. Both sit under AI.
wrong: Prediction from data is the textbook definition of machine learning, which is AI.
Generating new text is generative AI, which is AI.
Deep learning is one technique inside ML. Plenty of AI isn't deep learning.

practice.q: A retailer wants a system that reads a customer's request, searches inventory, places the order, and emails a confirmation without a person stepping in between. Which term BEST describes this system?
practice.why: Multi-step, goal-directed, uses tools (search, order, email), and acts on its own: that's an agent.
wrong: An LLM generates text. It might sit inside the agent, but the LLM alone doesn't place orders.
Computer vision interprets images; nothing here is visual.
Regression predicts a number. This system takes actions.

practice.q: A payroll department wants to replace its tax-withholding calculation with an AI model to 'modernize.' The calculation must produce the exact legally required amount every time. What should a consultant recommend?
a: Use a deep learning model trained on past paychecks.
Use a generative AI assistant to compute each amount.
Keep rule-based software; AI is not appropriate when a specific exact outcome is required.
Use a classification model to pick the right tax bracket.
practice.why: The exam guide lists 'situations when a specific outcome is needed instead of a prediction' as a case where AI/ML is not appropriate. Tax withholding is a fixed rule.
wrong: A model predicts; it can be wrong. Payroll can't be approximately right.
Generative AI can produce different answers to the same question. Worst possible fit.
Even a perfect bracket classifier doesn't compute the exact amount, and the rule is already known.

practice.q: A logistics company wants to predict how many minutes each delivery will take so drivers can be scheduled. Which type of machine learning problem is this?
practice.why: The answer is a number on a continuous scale (minutes), so it's regression.
wrong: Classification picks a category, like 'late' or 'on time'. The question asks for minutes.
Clustering finds groups in unlabeled data. There's a clear target here.
NLP is about text. There's no text to understand.

practice.q: A bank wants to flag incoming credit card transactions as either legitimate or fraudulent. Which ML technique fits BEST?
practice.why: Two labels, pick one for each transaction: classification. Fraud detection is also one of the exam's named real-world applications.
wrong: Regression outputs a number. 'Fraud or not' is a label.
Clustering could find odd groups, but the bank already knows the two categories it wants.
Summarization is a generative AI use case for text.

practice.q: An online store has purchase histories for millions of shoppers but no predefined customer categories. Marketing wants to discover natural groups of similar shoppers to target. Which technique fits?
practice.why: No labels, and the goal is to find groups the data suggests: clustering.
wrong: Classification needs known categories to assign. There aren't any yet.
Regression predicts a quantity. Nothing is being predicted.
Agents take actions. This is analysis of existing data.

practice.q: A hospital's radiologists review 4,000 scans a week and are behind. A proposed AI tool would highlight scans most likely to show a problem so radiologists see those first. Which value of AI/ML does this BEST illustrate?
a: Assisting human decision making and improving scalability
Reducing the need for medical data
practice.why: The tool prioritizes; humans still decide. The exam guide lists 'assist human decision making' and 'solution scalability' as core sources of AI/ML value.
wrong: Radiologists still make the call. The tool orders the queue.
AI predicts likelihoods. It can't guarantee a diagnosis, and a scenario promising guarantees is a red flag.
ML needs data; it doesn't reduce the need for it.

practice.q: Which of the following is NOT an example of a real-world AI application as listed in the AIF-C01 exam guide?
a: A system that recommends products based on past purchases
A system that transcribes spoken customer calls into text
A spreadsheet formula that sums monthly expenses
A system that forecasts next quarter's demand
practice.why: A sum is a fixed rule with one exact answer. The other three are named exam applications: recommendation systems, speech recognition, and forecasting.
wrong: Recommendation systems are a listed AI application.
Speech recognition is a listed AI application.
Forecasting is a listed AI application.

notTested.why: The exam only covers today's narrow AI. We teach the difference so the word AI never means robots in your head, but no question will ask about AGI or ASI.
